objectives:
This course explores the making of modern East Asia through the lenses of critical historiographical turns, archipelagic thinking, and the politics of embodiment. Moving beyond nation-centered narratives, the course examines how empire, colonial modernity, and shifting spatial imaginaries shaped lived experiences across Taiwan, Japan/Okinawa, Korean Peninsula, Hong Kong, and the wider Pacific world.
This course consists of three sections: (1)Archipelagic Turn, (2) Bodies under Empire (3) Spatializing East Asia. We begin by situating postwar intellectual transformations within the broader “cultural turn” in historical studies, drawing on Geoff Eley and debates on colonial modernity. The course then develops an “Archipelagic Turn,” engaging with the Black Atlantic, Pacific Rim discourses, and critiques of area studies to reconsider East Asia as a fluid, interconnected space rather than a fixed geopolitical entity.
The second section “Bodies under Empire” investigates how imperial power operated through hunger, health, reproduction, and racialization. Topics include starvation science and geopolitics, eugenics and total war, colonial governance in Taiwan and Hong Kong, and the Okinawan experience of the “Cycad Hell.” Here, the body becomes a crucial site where empire materializes through regulation, deprivation, and survival.
The final section “Spatializing East Asia” brings the course into direct dialogue with its central themes of empire, body, and spatial politics. Rather than treating war as a discrete event, this section examines how imperial power reorganizes space—through caves, camps, and infrastructures of confinement—and how these spaces, in turn, shape embodied experience. From the caves (gama) of Okinawa to prisoner-of-war camps in Southeast Asia, we explore how landscapes become technologies of survival, coercion, and memory. Engaging with the idea of a “liquid” East Asia, the course ultimately approaches the region not as a fixed geopolitical container but as an archipelagic formation—an interconnected yet fractured field shaped by imperial mobility, displacement, and contested spatial orders. By tracing the entanglement of bodies and spaces under empire, this course invites students to rethink East Asia as a dynamic configuration of power, movement, and lived experience.
